steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the main ways RNA and DNA differ:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (lacking one oxygen atom).  
   • RNA contains ribose (has an extra 2’-OH group), which makes RNA more reactive and less stable.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine.

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically a long, double-stranded helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.

4. Stability  
   • DNA’s deoxyribose and double-helix make it chemically stable—ideal for long-term genetic storage.  
   • RNA’s extra hydroxyl group and single strand make it more prone to hydrolysis—suited for temporary roles.

5. Cellular location  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA resides primarily in the nucleus (and in mitochondria/plastids).  
   • RNA is made in the nucleus but functions in both nucleus and cytoplasm.

6. Primary functions  
   • DNA stores and faithfully transmits the genetic blueprint from generation to generation.  
   • RNA plays diverse roles—messengers (mRNA), adaptors (tRNA), structural/catalytic components of ribosomes (rRNA), and many regulatory or catalytic RNAs (e.g., microRNA, ribozymes).

In short, DNA is the stable repository of hereditary information, while RNA is the more versatile, transient molecule that carries, translates, and regulates that information in the cell.
